result.title: Preface
result.summary: The Teachers’ Retirement System of the State of Illinois issued a request for proposals for private equity investment consultant services on August 7, 2024; responses were due at 2:00 p.m. CDT on September 4, 2024. The document covers the introduction, TRS overview, required services, proposal content and submission, evaluation process, anticipated timeline, and general conditions. Appendices include a vendor type verification form, minimum qualifications statement, reference authorization letter, questionnaire, fee proposal, and sample agreement.

result.title: I.  INTRODUCTION
result.summary: The Teachers’ Retirement System of Illinois (TRS) seeks competitive proposals from qualified firms for private equity investment consulting services to support prudent investment decisions. Proposals will be evaluated objectively and may lead to a consulting contract. TRS encourages qualified minority-, female-, disabled-, and veteran-owned firms to apply, consistent with financial and fiduciary prudence. Submitting a proposal or participating in presentations or negotiations does not obligate TRS to award a contract or reimburse costs. Proposals and related materials will be retained and may be disclosed under the Illinois Freedom of Information Act.

result.title: II. SUMMARY DESCRIPTION OF TRS
result.summary: Established in 1939, the Illinois Teachers’ Retirement System (TRS) administers a multiple-employer public pension plan providing retirement, disability, and death benefits. Membership is mandatory for eligible Illinois public school personnel outside Chicago and certain education-related state employees. As of March 31, 2024, TRS served over 448,000 members and held $70.40 billion in trust assets. It is a qualified plan governed by the Internal Revenue Code and Articles 1, 16, and 20 of the Illinois Pension Code, funded by member, employer, and state contributions and investment income. A Board of Trustees oversees the System; its Executive Director and staff manage daily operations. TRS is based in Springfield, with counseling in Lisle and an investment office in Chicago. Assets are invested by internal staff and external managers and consultants under fiduciary law and Board policy. The portfolio comprised equity (52.1%, $36.7 billion), income (27.1%, $19.1 billion), real assets (17.4%, $12.3 billion), and diversifying strategies (3.4%, $2.4 billion). Reports and information are available at trsil.org.

result.title: III. SERVICES REQUIRED
result.summary: The System seeks an experienced, ethical private equity consultant acting as a fiduciary under Board and executive direction. Duties include developing and reassessing the asset class, reviewing objectives, policies, markets, portfolio and performance, recommending sub-strategy targets, modeling pacing and exposures, delivering annual Board plans and reviews, evaluating investments across strategies and regions, advising on sales or replacements, and attending meetings. The consultant will report on market conditions and trends; provide strategy research and presentations; and support manager sourcing through a comprehensive database, quarterly opportunity heat maps, and monthly fundraising lists. It will conduct parallel, customized diligence against TRS criteria, review documents and track records, perform references/background checks, deliver detailed investment memos and recommendations, and advise on partnership agreement terms. Ongoing monitoring includes reviewing fund information, maintaining cash-flow and accounting records, quarterly detailed fund, co-investment and look-through performance reports, monthly capital-call and distribution reports, communicating with general partners, and advising on investment actions or agreement changes. Staff may also request research and other special projects.

result.title: IV. PROPOSAL CONTENT
result.summary: Proposals must use consecutively numbered pages, an indexed table of contents, and separate sections identified by index tabs; noncompliant formatting or false/misleading information may lead to rejection, and responses are verified. The signed business-letter cover letter must identify an authorized signer and include commitments to meet the RFP and keep the offer open through December 31, 2024; required election-business registration disclosures; anti-fraud, collusion, and remuneration certifications; disclosure of relevant TRS relationships or negotiations; agreement to Appendix F and acknowledgment that some state-mandated terms are nonnegotiable; acknowledgment of possible disclosure under Illinois FOIA and Open Meetings Act; and an accuracy attestation referencing potential felony penalties for falsification. Proposals must include completed Appendix A vendor verification and Appendix B minimum-qualification forms, an Appendix C reference authorization, the Appendix D questionnaire, and an Appendix E fee proposal covering all service expenses. The RFP is not a contract; selection may lead to negotiation based on Appendix F and the proposal. TRS may modify terms, but vendors should identify contractual concerns in their proposals or risk exclusion.

result.title: V. SUBMISSION OF PROPOSALS
result.summary: Proposals must be emailed as Adobe Acrobat files to Holly Walton at bidsubmissions@trsil.org by 2:00 P.M. CDT Wednesday, September 4, 2024; late submissions will be rejected. The subject line must identify the response and responder as specified, or the proposal may be rejected. Only email submissions are accepted; paper submissions are non-conforming, and TRS is not responsible for improperly labeled proposals. Receipt will be confirmed by email. Submitted proposals become TRS property, and proposers bear all costs of preparing proposals and attending presentations or interviews. Only one proposal per individual, vendor, partnership, corporation, or combination will be considered.

result.title: VI. EVALUATION PROCESS
result.summary: TRS first checks whether proposals include all required submittals in the prescribed format; incomplete proposals are rejected. Timely proposals that pass this review are assessed by TRS staff against minimum requirements and for best fit and value. Factors, in no ranked order, include understanding of requested services, approach and service quality, firm and assigned-staff qualifications, deliverables, and cost; cost matters but is not the primary determinant. TRS may request clarifications or additional information, but proposers cannot otherwise change or supplement proposals after the deadline. Requested information must be sent to bidsubmissions@trsil.org, not directly to evaluators. Selected finalists may be invited to roughly one-hour interviews or presentations, in person in Chicago or Springfield or virtually, and may present to the Board of Trustees at a public meeting. TRS does not reimburse related costs. It may require contract and fee negotiations before interviews or presentations, and may request a best-and-final fee offer at its discretion.

result.title: VIII. GENERAL CONDITIONS
result.summary: The section sets rules for RFP questions and communications: questions and error reports must be sent in writing to the designated contact by stated deadlines; answers or amendments may be posted online, and unauthorized contact or sharing proposal contents may lead to disqualification. TRS may reject proposers with defaults or poor performance, including related firms formed to evade a finding, and reject false claims or unsupported references. It may withdraw the RFP, reject proposals, or waive immaterial defects, but need not award a contract, reimburse proposal costs, or obtain services exclusively through this RFP. Proposals may be disclosed under Illinois FOIA; proposers may provide justified redactions and bear responsibility for them. TRS affirms equal opportunity and nondiscrimination. It may seek clarifications, negotiate with proposers, select the most advantageous offer rather than the lowest price, end negotiations, cancel, make no award, or reissue the RFP. Appendix A requires a signed vendor-type verification identifying qualifying women-, minority-, disability-, veteran-owned, combined, or other businesses.

nodes.title: RFP Questions and Communication Restrictions
nodes.summary: Proposers should submit RFP questions in writing to Holly Walton at Purchasing@trsil.org by noon CDT on August 19, 2024, using the specified subject line. TRS will not reply individually; if it chooses to respond, it will post questions and answers on its website by 4:30 p.m. CDT on August 23, 2024. Proposers must not contact TRS staff about the RFP except through this Q&A process. Any discovered errors should be reported promptly in writing to the same contact. TRS may clarify or modify the RFP by website notice before the proposal deadline. Proposers must not share proposal contents with other potential proposers. TRS policy and Illinois ethics law restrict communications during the search, and unauthorized contact with TRS staff or Trustees may result in disqualification.

nodes.title: C. Prior Deficiencies
nodes.summary: TRS may disqualify proposers with deficient performance, defaults, or prior failures to perform, unless deficiencies were beyond their reasonable control; newly formed firms linked to a previously non-responsible proposer must show they were not created to evade that finding. TRS may withdraw the RFP, accept or reject proposals, and waive immaterial defects without relaxing compliance requirements. False or misleading claims or unsupported references result in rejection. The RFP creates no duty to award a contract or reimburse proposal costs, and does not prevent TRS from obtaining similar services elsewhere. Proposals are generally subject to disclosure under Illinois FOIA; confidentiality labels alone do not protect them. Proposers may submit a redacted copy, must justify exemptions and redactions, and bear sole responsibility for doing so. TRS does not discriminate based on the listed characteristics—including race, religion, sex, age, disability, and military status—or any other characteristic.

nodes.title: Proposal Eligibility, TRS Rights, and Public Disclosure
nodes.summary: TRS may reject proposers in default on debts, contracts, or obligations, or with a record of poor performance; newly formed businesses linked to a previously non-responsible proposer may be disqualified unless they show they were not created to evade that finding. TRS may withdraw the RFP, accept or reject proposals, and waive immaterial irregularities without excusing full compliance. False or misleading claims or unsupported references will result in rejection. The RFP creates no duty to award a contract or reimburse proposal costs, and does not prevent TRS from obtaining similar services elsewhere. Proposals are generally subject to disclosure under Illinois FOIA; confidentiality labels alone do not prevent disclosure. Proposers may submit a redacted copy with the unredacted proposal, representing that redactions qualify for FOIA exemptions. They must justify challenged redactions in writing; TRS need not help determine whether exemptions apply.

F. Equal Opportunity
TRS does not discriminate because of actual or perceived race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, age, marital status, pregnancy, order of protection status, military status, certain unfavorable discharges from military service, political affiliation, citizenship, ancestry, national origin, physical or mental disability, genetic information, or any other characteristic
12protected by law. It is the System’s intent to comply with all state, federal, and local equal employment opportunity laws and public policies.

nodes.title: G. Selection, Negotiation, Additional Information
nodes.summary: TRS need not accept the lowest-priced proposal and may negotiate with any proposer or request clarification or additional information. It will select the offer most advantageous based on evaluation factors beyond price. Before award, TRS may negotiate with the highest-ranked respondents to resolve service differences, clarify details and responsibilities, emphasize issues, obtain assurances, and improve the contract. If no agreement is reached after three days, TRS may end negotiations and approach another responsive proposer. TRS may also cancel the RFP at any time, make no award, or reissue it with changes if doing so is in its best interest.

result.title: APPENDIX C: REFERENCE AUTHORIZATION LETTER
result.summary: Appendix C is a template reference authorization letter for a prospective vendor, with placeholders for letterhead, date, recipient, and vendor details. It states that the vendor has proposed private equity investment consulting services to the Illinois Teachers’ Retirement System (System), which is conducting due diligence. The vendor authorizes any person or entity to provide the System with information about the vendor, its principals, employees, and agents. A copy may be treated as an original. The letter closes with thanks, a vendor signature and title, and a cc to R. Stanley Rupnik, CFA, Executive Director and CIO of TRS.

result.title: APPENDIX D: QUESTIONNAIRE
result.summary: Requires vendors to complete and return the questionnaire in its stated order, beginning with contact and identification details. It covers firm and parent history, ownership, services, revenue, assets, legal and regulatory matters, compensation sources, client history and references, and potential conflicts. It asks about personnel, expertise, staffing and capacity, proposed TRS leadership, diversity and turnover, discretionary-account capabilities, technology, compensation, and experience across private-equity strategies, regions, and sectors. Portfolio-construction questions address policy, allocation, returns, strategy and market views, analytics, tactical positioning, funds-of-funds, smaller managers, secondaries, opportunity allocation, and co-investments, with supporting exhibits. Sourcing questions cover databases, pipeline and opportunity volumes, geographic and sector coverage, manager selection and approvals, diligence and conflict controls, legal review, and ongoing monitoring of compliance, cash flows, fees, performance, risk, portfolio companies, reporting, audits, systems, vendor tools, and integration with total-portfolio risk analysis.

nodes.title: B. General Firm Information
nodes.summary: Requests information on the firm’s and parent organization’s history and significant changes over the past five years; future private equity consulting plans, account and asset capacity, and staffing growth; other services, ownership structure (Exhibit #1), and consulting’s share of revenue; relevant litigation, legal proceedings, and regulatory investigations and outcomes; any direct or indirect compensation from investment managers or general partners; all business lines, assets under management, and revenue sources; and a five-year client list detailing account type, private equity assets, mandate scope, responsibilities, relationship status and duration, and reasons for departing clients. It also requests four new client mandates and three client losses or unsuccessful RFPs as references (Exhibit #10), potential conflicts arising from a TRS engagement—including client relationships and discretionary fund-of-funds investing—and the firm’s approach to conflicts and scale issues in discretionary accounts.

nodes.title: C. Depth and Experience of Personnel
nodes.summary: The section asks firms to describe their alternative-investment consulting strengths, limitations, staffing, key private-equity issues for public pensions, and consulting innovations, naming key contributors. It requests organization size; key professionals’ titles, tenure, consulting and direct-investment experience; and proposed TRS account leadership, other assignments, time commitment, location, backup, maximum caseload, and biographies. Firms must report workforce and TRS-team representation of minorities, women, people with disabilities, and veterans, plus five-year technical/support and management/professional turnover, including names and replacements. It covers discretionary-account capabilities in investment pipelines, diligence, monitoring, and co-investor relationships; staffing and technology for an online GP-record repository; and professional compensation’s role in retention and aligned interests. Firms should detail private-equity experience across venture, buyouts, market sizes, regions, sector specialists, fund-of-funds, secondaries, and distressed or restructuring strategies, and provide an expertise-based organizational chart spanning investment strategies, subsectors, geographies, and sectors.

nodes.title: D. Portfolio Construction
nodes.summary: Requests a description of the firm’s portfolio-construction process, including client analysis, investment policy, asset allocation, and expected returns; views on growth versus value by strategy, geography, sector, and asset size; portfolio analytics, an example exhibit, and their use in assessing managers; and tactical positioning, when it is appropriate, and engagement examples. It asks about funds-of-funds, small managers’ potential to outperform larger platforms (with supporting data) and how large programs can access them, plus experience with secondary acquisitions and divestitures. Requested exhibits include 2019–2021 recommendations for primary funds under $5 billion, categorized by vintage, strategy, geography, and sector. It also covers client opportunity allocation, resolving allocation issues and reporting outcomes, and the role of co-investments and their integration with primary fund selection and portfolio diversification.

nodes.title: E. Sourcing
nodes.summary: The text requests information on the firm’s sourcing capabilities: investment tracking by alternative sector, fund size, manager count, performance history, geographic coverage, data sources, and sample reports; annual opportunity volumes and fund reviews by strategy; pipeline development and historically successful firms across Europe, Asia, Australia, sectors, and WMBE managers; sourcing smaller buyout funds, heat maps, client-specific opportunities, and recent resource or database enhancements. It asks for investment selection criteria, manager evaluation standards, approvals, diligence questionnaire and client-report examples, conflict mitigation, and legal diligence, including in-house and external counsel. Monitoring topics include LPA and GP compliance, cash flows, fees and carry, verification, performance methodologies and benchmarks, market research, reporting timelines and delivery, report samples, audit support, GP evaluation, risk aggregation, portfolio-company analytics and client access, system pros and cons, vendor licenses and TRS access, and experience integrating private equity holdings into total-portfolio risk tools, including relevant personnel.

result.title: Appendix E: Fee Proposal
result.summary: Appendix E requests a hard-dollar fee proposal and scope of services for: (A) annual full-service private equity consulting; (B) annual quarterly performance measurement and portfolio monitoring reports; (C) manager searches; (D) hourly special-project or service rates; and (E) ancillary services such as legal reviews and stock distribution management. It asks whether the firm and its employees or owners will agree not to receive any direct or indirect commissions or fees arising from securities invested in by TRS; whether travel for Board and onsite meetings is included; what additional value-adding services are available outside the proposal and their fees; and whether the firm offers bundled full-retainer consulting fees across multiple asset classes.

result.title: Appendix F: [Sample] Master Services Agreement
result.summary: Appendix F presents a sample Master Services Agreement between Illinois TRS and a contractor, with placeholders, recitals, incorporated definitions, appointment, scope and governing documents, and a nonextendable term ending December 31, 2029. It sets fixed fees, invoicing and audit rules; contractor duties, fiduciary and legal compliance, confidentiality, reporting, extensive warranties and certifications, insurance, indemnity, records, subcontractor and assignment controls, and independent, nonexclusive status. It covers termination and transition, System ownership of deliverables and licenses for embedded pre-existing materials, publicity limits, and other operational, legal and employment provisions. Definitions clarify key service, work, documentation, data and intellectual-property terms. The Data Security Addendum imposes safeguards for System Information, including access controls, encryption, audits, incident response, subcontractor controls, remediation, and specified costs and indemnity. Exhibit C is TRS’s investment policy, addressing mission, roles, implementation, allocation, manager selection and oversight, transitions, benchmarks, risk, restrictions, monitoring, proxy voting, brokerage, sustainability, access, emerging managers and loss recovery.

nodes.title: 2. Services:
nodes.summary: Appendix F provides a sample Master Services Agreement for a private equity investment consultant between the Illinois Teachers’ Retirement System (TRS) and a contractor, with placeholders for the date, contractor name, legal status, and address. The recitals describe the Master Trust, TRS’s aim to obtain consulting services for its defined benefit assets and prudently manage trust assets, and the contractor’s qualification through the RFP process. The agreement incorporates Exhibit A for undefined capitalized terms and appoints the contractor as consultant and investment adviser. Services must comply with the agreement, the August 7, 2024 RFP, the contractor’s RFP response, and Exhibit C investment policy, under direction of designated TRS officials; specific work is left to be agreed. Software deliverables’ support, maintenance, and service levels are to be specified in the RFP, if applicable. Services run from execution through December 31, 2029, for no more than five years, subject to earlier termination, and the term cannot be extended.

nodes.title: 4. Compensation:
nodes.summary: The agreement sets fixed, generally nonreimbursable fees; quarterly, supported and timely invoices; payment, tax, accounting and audit rules. Contractor must comply with Illinois and other applicable laws, current investment policies, fiduciary duties, confidentiality and data-security requirements, and provide disclosures, periodic reports and annual performance-review cooperation. It gives extensive warranties and certifications covering qualified performance, intellectual property, software security, adviser registration, personnel, conflicts, ethics, procurement eligibility, labor, nondiscrimination and other statutory matters. It addresses authorization, Illinois law and courts, sovereign immunity, amendments, notices, entire-agreement priority, severability, counterparts and survival. Contractor is independent, nonexclusive, must maintain insurance, indemnify the System, retain auditable records, and obtain consent for assignment or substitutions; subcontractors are bound by the agreement. Termination includes mutual, breach and System convenience rights, with transition and payment provisions. Deliverables belong to the System, with licenses for embedded pre-existing materials; publicity is restricted. The agreement also covers employee non-solicitation, bankruptcy notice, security on premises, finder’s fees, inability to perform and cumulative remedies.

nodes.title: DEFINITIONS
nodes.summary: Defines Deliverables (including Documentation), Documentation, Good Industry Practice, Intellectual Property Rights, Personal Data, Pre-Existing IP, Pre-Existing Contractor Materials, Services, and Work. The Data Security Addendum requires stronger applicable legal/industry safeguards or listed minimum controls when Contractor or its third parties handle System Information, which is confidential and restricted to contract purposes. Requirements cover access controls and MFA; written security policies, passwords, encryption, backups, logging, vulnerability remediation, supported systems, ISO 27001 security programs, continuity and disaster recovery, legal compliance, U.S.-only data handling unless approved, personnel screening, and subcontractor restrictions and liability. It mandates annual independent security audits, report delivery and remediation, incident notification, cooperation, mitigation, legally required breach reporting, Contractor-paid response costs when Contractor is responsible, and indemnification for specified direct losses. Exhibit C is the Illinois Teachers’ Retirement System Investment Policy, adopted in 2000 and revised July 1, 2024; its contents cover mission and purpose, investment philosophy and roles, consultant notifications, implementation, allocation, manager selection and oversight, transitions, benchmarks, custody risk, restrictions, monitoring, proxy voting, brokerage, sustainability, access, emerging managers, and recovery of investment losses.

result.title: I. Mission Statement and Core Values
result.summary:
I. Mission Statement and Core Values
The Board of Trustees (“Board”) of the Teachers’ Retirement System of the State of Illinois (“TRS”, “System”) has a fiduciary responsibility to the Members and Beneficiaries of the System. In recognition of this responsibility, the Board has adopted the following Mission Statement:
TRS’s Mission Statement
Delivering expert pension service to Illinois public educators as they earn their promised retirement security.
TRS’s Core Values
• Integrity: We are tenaciously honest and ethical.
• Accountability: We openly set high standards and confidently own our actions and results.
• Service: We genuinely care for our members and each other by being kind and helpful.
• Teamwork: We proudly collaborate as one TRS.
• Diversity: We are inclusive and persistently embrace our differences to empower our success.
• Continuous Improvement: We challenge ourselves to embrace learning, new ideas and growth.
Page 3Investment Policy July 1, 2024

result.title: II. Statement of Purpose of Investment Policy
result.summary: The policy defines TRS’s investment philosophy and practices as guidance for managing System assets and supporting participants’ financial security through a long-term plan of prudent investment. It is an official policy; deviations require advance written Board permission. The Board and Staff acknowledge fiduciary duties under the Illinois Pension Code: fiduciaries include those controlling or advising the System; they must act solely to provide benefits and pay administrative expenses, use prudent-expert care and skill, diversify to limit large losses unless imprudent, comply with the Code, and avoid prohibited transactions or conflicts of interest. These statutory duties underpin three guiding principles: preserve the Trust’s long-term principal, maximize total return within prudent risk limits, and act exclusively for members and beneficiaries.

result.title: III. Investment Philosophy
key_items:  TRS's Total Fund Investment Return Objective
 The goal of TRS's investment strategy is to achieve a total rate of return of at least 7.00 percent per annum.
result.summary: TRS’s investment objective is to maintain liquid reserves for promised benefits, funded by state and school district contributions, member contributions, and investment returns; continued state contributions are assumed. The Board targets a total annual investment return of at least 7%. Its long-term risk philosophy accepts prudent risk for potential reward, uses diversification to control risk, recognizes equities’ long-term return potential and fixed income’s role in reducing volatility and providing liquidity, and prioritizes strategic asset allocation over short-term tactical shifts. The Board sets allocation based on objectives, fiduciary and statutory duties, financial condition, liquidity, funding sources, and economic conditions. Staff and the Investment Committee regularly monitor volatility, equity beta, risk-adjusted returns, downside performance, and liquidity; non-liquidity measures are compared with the policy index and peers. Diversification spans asset classes, geography, industries, and maturities, with internal or external managers selected under Board-approved allocations informed by staff and consultants. Formal reviews occur quarterly for total-fund performance; every three years for asset allocation; and annually for asset-class structure, policy, consultants, managers, and custodian.

result.title: IV. Role Definitions
result.summary: The section clarifies fiduciary roles to support efficient administration, clear accountability, and avoid duplicated work. The Board sets System-wide policies, oversees prudent use of assets, acts on investment recommendations, and approves actuarial assumptions, contribution rates, and plan-administration policies. Its Investment Committee recommends investment policies and actions, including allocation, managers, benchmarks, custody, lending, and service providers, and reviews operations; an optional working group may discuss and review matters but cannot direct, act, or vote. The Board-appointed CIO administers investments, monitors performance and policy compliance, communicates with Board leaders, improves procedures, and safeguards assets. Internal staff supports analysis, implementation, monitoring, and recommendations, collaborating with Board-hired consultants who provide independent advice; procedures, annual reviews, and escalation of unresolved differences provide checks and balances. Board-appointed external managers invest within written mandates and report performance. The Custodian safeguards assets, collects income, reports holdings and performance, allocates cash as directed, and may support lending. Legal Counsel reviews specified documents and legal matters, not investment merits or decisions.

nodes.title: Board of Trustees
nodes.summary:
IV. Role Definitions
TRS is one of the larger public pension funds in the United States, as such its operational requirements are complex. The Board relies heavily on both Internal Staff and external contractors in order to properly administer the System and implement its investment strategies. Because of the number of parties involved, their roles as fiduciaries must be clearly identified to increase operational efficiency, to ensure clear lines of responsibility, and to reduce or eliminate duplication of effort.
Board of Trustees
The Board has the responsibility of establishing and maintaining broad policies and objectives for all aspects of the System’s operation. The Board is responsible for prudent investment and expenditure of the System’s funds and assets. Specifically with regard to investments, the Board takes action upon recommendations that come from its Investment Committee. The Board also approves actuarial assumptions, certifies contribution rates and determines policies pertaining to the administration of the plans and benefits under its jurisdiction and responsibility.

nodes.title: Investment Committee
nodes.summary: The Board establishes the Investment Committee and elects its Chair and Vice Chair. The Committee recommends investment actions to the Board on investment-program policies (including investment, rebalancing, manager hiring and termination, brokerage, proxy voting, and securities class-action policies), asset allocation and asset-class/tactical plans, benchmarks, the custodian relationship, securities lending, investment managers, consultants, and other service providers. It meets before regular Board meetings to review investment activities; staff and consultants brief it on relevant operations and results and recommend actions. At its discretion, the Board may create an informal Investment Working Group to improve transparency and enable more frequent Trustee–staff communication. The group gathers information only and cannot direct, act, or vote, but may discuss investment actions and review them for consistency with Board policies and internal procedures.

nodes.title: Chief Investment Officer
nodes.summary:
Chief Investment Officer
The Chief Investment Officer (“CIO”) is appointed by and serves at the pleasure of the Board. The CIO is responsible for planning, organizing, and administering the investment operations of the System under broad policy guidance and direction from the Board. The CIO, with assistance of Investment Staff, monitors the performance of the investment portfolio; ensures that funds are invested in accordance with Board policies; communicates with the Board, its Officers and the Investment Committee Chair and Vice Chair; studies, recommends, and implements policy and operational procedures that will enhance the investment program of TRS; and ensures that proper internal controls are developed to safeguard the assets of the System. In fulfilling these investment responsibilities, the CIO relies heavily on the Internal Investment Staff and Consultant(s).

nodes.title: Internal Investment Staff
nodes.summary: Internal Investment Staff reports to the CIO and supports the Board and Investment Committee through manager monitoring, possible internal management, consulting, asset-allocation analysis and rebalancing, implementation of Board decisions, manager-selection advice, industry liaison, and updates on relevant financial, economic, and sociopolitical developments. Reporting follows Investment Policy and Board or Committee direction. Staff works with external consultants, generally developing Committee recommendations jointly; work may be led by the party with greater expertise. Staff recommendations are developed through oversight committees governed by procedures typically reviewed annually to promote prudent, consistent decisions. Consultants are hired by and report to the Board, providing independent perspectives on the Fund’s goals, structure, performance, and managers; reviewing allocations and performance; advising on manager selection; and promptly reporting material manager changes. The Board may retain specialist consultants, whose performance is reviewed annually and before renewal. Staff-consultant collaboration provides checks and balances: recommendations are generally joint, differences should usually be resolved professionally, and unresolved views are brought to the Chair for guidance and communication with other members.

nodes.title: External Investment Managers
nodes.summary:
External Investment Managers
The external Investment Managers (“Managers”) serve at the pleasure of the Board. The Staff and Consultant will provide the Managers with explicit written directions detailing their particular assignments. They will select, buy, and sell specific securities or investments within the parameters specified by Staff and Consultant and in adherence to this Investment Policy or to other policies set forth by the Board. Managers will construct and manage investment portfolios that are consistent with the investment philosophy and disciplines for which the Board hired them. Certain Managers may also, at the direction of the Board, engage in a Securities Lending program. Discretion is delegated to the Managers to carry out these investment actions. Managers will provide performance reporting to the Staff utilizing standardized reporting formats and at intervals specified by Staff.

nodes.title: Custodian
nodes.summary: The Board selects the Custodian, who serves at its pleasure. The Custodian collects income, safeguards cash and securities, and regularly reports holdings and individual and combined performance to Staff, providing data and performance reports to Staff and the Consultant at intervals set by policy or contract. A bank or trust depository holds incoming cash before allocation and invests it in liquid, interest-bearing instruments. To maintain Board-authorized asset-allocation targets, Staff directs the Custodian to allocate cash or securities to Investment Managers as needed. At the Board’s direction, the Custodian may conduct securities lending; if additional lending agents are used, the Custodian must cooperate and provide requested reporting.

nodes.title: Office of Legal Counsel
nodes.summary: The Office of Legal Counsel reviews draft documents and advises on legal issues to protect the System, checking business terms for form and legality but not assessing investment or financial merits or approving investment decisions. Staff must bring it documents for the Executive Director’s signature; new or amended investment management agreements, provider contracts, letters and side letters; requests for proposals; nondisclosure/confidentiality agreements; revisions to the approved IMA master or investment policies; and termination letters. It also handles matters Investment Staff refers to outside counsel, except routine matters the CIO may address directly; disclosures or discoveries of legal, SEC, administrative, or investigatory proceedings involving current or prospective managers or key personnel; correspondence concerning actual or potential litigation or legal issues; and material contractual violations by managers or providers, excluding investment-parameter violations.

result.title: V. Consultant Notification Process
result.summary: Staff and the Consultant work together to report on investment performance and manager due diligence and recommend opportunities for the System. Because investment decisions involve qualitative judgment, checks and balances help assure the Board that their collective recommendations serve the System’s best interests. Both Staff and the Consultant monitor policy implementation. The Board requires the Consultant to act independently and notify the CIO, Director, Board Chair, and Board, as appropriate, in writing of investment-related concerns or issues and recommendations.

result.title: VI. Implementation
result.summary: TRS’s complex investment operations require daily attention, which the Board and Committee cannot provide through periodic meetings. The Board therefore delegates operational duties to various parties, with efficiency depending on clear assignments and coordination among those identified in Section IV. The Investment Policy serves as a broad, enduring guide to implementing TRS’s investment philosophy and practices. Detailed matters—including asset allocation, manager structure and parameters, and cost management—are omitted because of their complexity and volume; Investment Staff maintain these details and provide them to the Board upon request.

result.title: VII. Asset Allocation and Rebalancing Strategy
result.summary: The Board’s allocation policy seeks to meet or exceed investment objectives at a controlled level of risk, considering the System’s capacity for volatility and changes in financial condition, asset-class risk and return, correlations, and liability effects. The four classes are equity, real assets, diversifying strategies, and income. Long-term/interim targets are 52%/52% equity (37%/37% public, 15%/15% private), 18%/18% real assets (16%/16% real estate, 2%/2% other), 6%/5% diversifying strategies, and 24%/25% income (15%/15% global income, 8%/8% private credit, 1%/2% short-term). Targets are reviewed annually and formally studied at least every three years. Rebalancing ranges allow modest deviations to manage risk, pursue opportunities, and limit costs; staff use cash flows to stay near targets and may rebalance public markets when limits or triggers are reached. Plans account for market conditions, liquidity, transaction costs, and investment horizons, with advance advice to Board leadership for actions outside authorized limits and regular reporting to the Investment Committee.

nodes.title: Asset Allocation and Rebalancing Strategy
nodes.summary: The System’s allocation policy aims to meet or exceed its investment objectives at a Board-approved, controlled level of risk, accounting for the plan’s ability to withstand volatility and changes in financial condition. The Board established four broad asset classes—equity, income, real assets, and diversifying strategies—and considered asset-class risk, return, correlations, and effects on liabilities when setting targets. Long-term and interim allocations, respectively, are: equity 52%/52% (public 37%/37%, private 15%/15%); real assets 18%/18% (real estate 16%/16%, other 2%/2%); diversifying strategies 6%/5%; and income 24%/25% (global income 15%/15%, private credit 8%/8%, short-term 1%/2%). Both mixes total 100%. Targets are reviewed annually and formally studied at least every three years.

nodes.title: Strategic Allocation Rebalancing Policy
nodes.summary: Rebalancing periodically shifts funds among assets or asset classes to restore target allocations. Systematic rebalancing helps maintain the Board-approved allocation and its long-term risk/return characteristics, while overly narrow ranges or frequent trades can create unnecessary costs. The Board uses allocation ranges rather than scheduled periods; ranges reflect each asset class’s volatility and share of the total fund. While allocations remain within limits, TRS Staff use available cash flow to stay as close to targets as possible. If an asset class breaches its limits, the public market fund may be actively rebalanced to target. The policy references ranges within a broader four-class risk structure and shows an equity section covering public and private equity, but the excerpt provides no range values.

nodes.title: Real Assets
nodes.summary:
Real Assets
Real Estate Other Real Assets

nodes.title: Diversifying Strategies Income
nodes.summary: The table sets lower, target, and upper allocation percentages for the fund’s asset classes, including diversifying strategies, income, global income, private credit, and short-term investments. If a public-market asset class reaches a trigger point, the fund may be rebalanced toward target allocations; exact short-term targets for less-liquid assets may be impractical, so timing and extent should account for transaction costs, liquidity needs, and investment horizons. Staff develops and implements rebalancing plans suited to market conditions, aiming to minimize costs and disruption, and advises the Chair and/or Vice Chair before activity outside Board-authorized limits. Even without a trigger, Staff may make minor adjustments to support effective implementation and maintain Board-approved exposures and portfolio structures. Rebalancing results are reported to the Investment Committee at regular meetings.

nodes.title: Asset Class Rebalancing Range
nodes.summary:
Asset Class Rebalancing Range
Establishing a rebalancing range allows Staff to implement modest position variances relative to policy targets in order to control risk, adjust to market opportunities, and/or minimize fund transaction costs. The Board allows Staff the ability to rebalance public markets asset classes within the ranges indicated in this policy and tactical plans.
Page 16Investment Policy July 1, 2024

result.title: VIII. Investment Manager Structure
result.summary: The Board sets strategic portfolio structure and authorizes Staff to use external managers and diversify across asset classes. Staff and the Consultant define asset-class structures through tactical plans or annual reviews for Board approval; they may use multiple managers per mandate and adjust weightings for risk, cost, or performance, with all structure revisions subject to the applicable Staff Oversight Committee’s approval. Managers receive tactical roles and may be evaluated on consistency of philosophy, style, and personnel; performance versus an appropriate benchmark or peer group; and net value added. Staff and the Consultant implement the strategy, supervise managers, monitor performance, and report to the Board on the Section III schedule, when requested, or as they deem necessary. To diversify managers, no active firm—including its parent and affiliates, subsidiaries, or joint ventures—may manage more than 10% of total fund assets. Market-driven excesses do not trigger automatic withdrawals, but prohibit further allocations through rebalancing or new mandates while the firm remains above the limit.

result.title: IX. Investment Manager Hiring Guidelines
result.summary: The guidelines require external investment-manager hiring to be transparent, competitive, objectively evaluated, documented, and solely in participants’ and beneficiaries’ best interests. Searches must address an approved new asset class or strategy, diversification, manager replacement, asset-class targets, or a superior alternative. Public- and private-market searches use role-specific criteria and due diligence, with candidates sourced, screened, and assessed for qualifications and strategic fit. Staff and the Consultant recommend candidates to the relevant oversight committee; selections and commitments must comply with Board allocations, policy, tactical plans, and limits, with required committee reporting. Co-investments receive separate due diligence and approval, while recommendations outside Board policy go to the Investment Committee. Provider selection compares qualified candidates, considers cost, verifies fair and consistent processes, and requires appropriate documentation and approved transaction documents. Search materials and due diligence must describe performance, risk, benchmarks, firms, funds, partners, terms, concerns, and suitability; expectations are incorporated into investment or partnership agreements. Staff and the Consultant monitor results, conduct periodic due diligence, report material events, and oversee private-market relationships. Contingent placement and related fees are prohibited.

nodes.title: Introduction
nodes.summary:
IX. Investment Manager Hiring Guidelines
Introduction
The Trustees of the Teachers' Retirement System (“TRS”) have established the following guidelines for hiring external investment managers. In establishing these guidelines, it is the Board’s intention to assure all interested parties that decisions made in carrying out these actions occur in a full disclosure environment characterized by competitive selection, objective evaluation, and proper documentation. The overriding consideration with respect to all decisions is that they shall be made solely in the best interest of plan participants and beneficiaries.
Clearly Defined Objectives
Any action to hire a manager should be based on one or more of the following observations:
• Identification of a new asset class or investment strategy which has been approved in advance by the Board.
• A need for diversification of styles within an existing asset class.
• A need to replace an investment manager terminated by the System or pending termination.
• A need to retain additional managers in order to reach an asset class target.
• A superior alternative to an incumbent has been discovered.

nodes.title: Search and Selection Process
nodes.summary: The policy establishes a consistent, competitive, due-diligence-based manager selection process, with implementation differences for public and private markets. Searches begin with role-specific criteria: public-market profiles set quantitative and qualitative requirements, with ongoing monitoring and formal screening for small/mid-cap equities; private-market annual tactical plans define strategy, criteria, and allocation targets. Candidates are identified from the Consultant’s database or market opportunities, screened for qualifications and strategic fit, and invited to submit RFP/RFI responses or private-market questionnaires. Staff and the Consultant recommend candidates to the applicable Staff Oversight Committee, supported by search documentation and compliance confirmation. Public-market selections and initial funding must follow Board-approved allocations; private-market commitments must fit tactical plans and limits, with post-funding or commitment reports to the Investment Committee. Co-investments undergo separate Staff due diligence and Oversight Committee approval. Recommendations outside Board policy go to the Investment Committee. Important managers may periodically present performance or market expertise to the Committee or Board.

nodes.title: Competitive Environment
nodes.summary: Investment service-provider selection should be open and competitive, comparing qualified providers where appropriate. Evaluation criteria are often subjective, except for passive index managers; cost is always considered but rarely controls the decision. For delegated hiring reviews, the Investment Committee and Board focus on compliance with the Pension Code, rules, and policy, and may request documentation disclosing the search, sourcing, and due diligence. Staff, the Consultant, and the oversight committee should verify that the process was fair and screening consistent. Candidates may be asked to present. Transaction documents must be finalized and approved by the Staff Oversight Committee; any exception for pending negotiations must be disclosed to the Investment Committee and noted in the related Board resolution.

nodes.title: Defining Expectations
nodes.summary: For public markets manager searches, the search document must summarize performance criteria, absolute and relative risks, staff’s qualitative assessment, and relevant benchmarks or peer comparisons. Staff and the Consultant must incorporate manager expectations into the executed Investment Management Agreement. For private markets investments, Committee due diligence must describe the firm, fund, and key partners; fund terms and conditions; key concerns and risks; and the investment’s suitability for the System’s tactical plan and portfolio. Staff must incorporate relevant manager expectations into the executed Partnership and Subscription Agreements.

nodes.title: Board Reporting and Monitoring
nodes.summary:
Board Reporting and Monitoring
After a manager is selected, the Staff and Consultant will regularly monitor the manager’s results versus expectations. The System’s Staff and Consultant will conduct periodic due diligence meetings with the outside organizations and are responsible for collaboration on relevant issues and reporting to the Board on any material events regarding an investment manager.
Oversight responsibilities within private market relationships include active participation on fund Advisory Boards (when TRS holds a seat on such Boards), periodic portfolio reviews, and appropriate attendance at partnership annual meetings.

nodes.title: Placement Fees
nodes.summary:
Placement Fees
The System does not permit the payment of third-party placement, marketing, solicitor’s, finder’s, consulting, or any other contingent fee in relation to the procurement of a TRS investment.
Page 22Investment Policy July 1, 2024

result.title: X. Investment Manager Retention Analysis
result.summary: The policy treats retention as important as selection, applying disciplined, timely, long-term assessment to TRS external managers while avoiding both prolonged underperformance and premature termination. Monitoring combines monthly custodian reports, quarterly manager reports, regular Staff/Consultant reports to the Investment Committee, and qualitative contact. Public-market and diversifying managers generally meet annually; passive managers biennially, with increased scrutiny as needed. Public-market managers may enter the Watch List after two consecutive quarters of net rolling three-year underperformance versus benchmark; poor returns alone do not require termination. Staff notify the Oversight Committee, monitor and review the manager, and recommend action; a subsequent period above benchmark generally removes the manager from the list. Material organizational, personnel, client, strategy, responsiveness, consultant, policy, or other concerns may also trigger review. Responses range from no action to termination, considering each case and transition costs. The framework guides decisions but mandates neither retention nor termination; the authorized committee decides collectively after consultation with Staff and/or the Consultant. Public-market contracts may be terminated immediately upon notice, with or without cause.

nodes.title: Monitoring and Evaluation Process
nodes.summary: The policy treats manager retention as equally important as initial selection and requires disciplined, timely decisions to avoid retaining persistent underperformers or terminating managers before rebounds. It applies to TRS external managers unless otherwise noted and aims to support long-term evaluation, statistically sound skill assessment, timely responses to performance concerns, and flexibility across asset classes, styles, and markets. Monitoring includes monthly custodian reports to Staff, quarterly standardized manager reports, and regular Staff/Consultant reports to the Investment Committee, supplemented by ongoing qualitative contact. Public-markets and diversifying-strategy managers generally receive annual meetings to review performance, strategy, organization, personnel, and process; passive managers are generally reviewed biennially. Staff may increase contact when concerns arise, the Consultant participates in many meetings and conducts ongoing monitoring, and the Committee or its Chair, Staff, or Consultant may call managers before the Board at any time.

nodes.title: Watch List and Termination Guidelines
key_items: Qualitative Factors Resulting in Watch List Addition and Recommended Actions
nodes.summary: Public market managers may be added to the Watch List when their net rolling three-year return is below the benchmark for two consecutive quarters; poor performance alone does not mandate termination. Staff then notify the Staff Oversight Committee, closely monitor the manager, may meet or formally re-interview them, and recommend a course of action at the next meeting. The manager remains listed pending review; one subsequent period above the benchmark generally leads to removal and restarts observation. Ongoing qualitative reviews cover investment style, philosophy, process, personnel, and organization. Material adverse events—such as ownership or structural changes, key-person losses, client or asset losses, strategy shifts, persistent unresponsiveness, consultant downgrades, policy violations, or other material concerns—may prompt Watch List placement and committee review, including a special meeting for serious issues. Responses may range from no action to Watch List placement, meetings, interview, comprehensive review, or termination. Decisions are case-specific, and termination should account for transition costs.

nodes.title: Conclusion
nodes.summary:
Conclusion
This Framework provides guidelines that are useful in determining the conditions under which a contract relationship between an investment manager and TRS should be called into question. In addition, circumstances are depicted in which Staff and/or the Board of Trustees may elect to terminate a manager for cause (all of TRS’s public market investment manager contracts may be terminated, with or without cause, immediately upon notification).
A manager retention decision is very important to the continued success of a pension fund’s investment strategy. As such, it should not be taken lightly nor should it be made with blind reliance on quantitative or qualitative guidelines. The ultimate decision rests in the collective judgment of the applicable Staff Oversight Committee, by granted authority of the Board of Trustees, following consultation with the responsible Staff and/or the Consultant. Nothing contained in this Investment Manager Retention Policy mandates retention or termination of an investment manager.
Page 25Investment Policy July 1, 2024

result.title: XI. Investment Manager Termination Guidelines
result.summary: The guidelines govern terminating investment managers as a business decision made solely in participants’ and beneficiaries’ best interests, with full disclosure, competitive bidding, objective evaluation, and documentation. Possible grounds include ownership or personnel changes, client or asset losses, changes in philosophy or responsiveness, TRS strategy or policy changes, poor performance, approved new asset classes, diversification needs, or a superior alternative; the list is not exhaustive. Each case requires identified considerations and a tailored quantitative and qualitative evaluation. Records should explain the rationale, relevant issues, assumptions, results, and, where appropriate, risks, costs, and expected benefits. With Staff Oversight Committee approval, Staff and Consultant may initiate termination when a manager no longer fits the System’s allocation or asset-class structure, documenting their rationale. Assets may go to a search finalist, other TRS managers, passive management, or cash needs; the Investment Committee and Board receive a report. The Investment Committee reviews whether decisions were prudent, well reasoned, fair, and consistently applied; members may request supporting records. A manager may be invited to present, but this cannot delay Board action.

result.title: XII. Transition Management
key_items: Definitions; Objective; Transition Manager Pool Selection Process
Transition Manager Assignment / Scope of Services
result.summary: Transition management moves securities from a legacy to a target portfolio while controlling timing, costs and benchmark exposure; it can cover manager changes, interim management, rebalancing, cash flows and strategy changes. Implementation shortfall measures total explicit costs (commissions, fees, taxes) and implicit costs (spreads, market impact and opportunity cost). TRS seeks timely, cost-effective transitions that maintain appropriate exposure and minimize total shortfall. Staff administer a competitively selected, Staff Oversight Committee-approved manager pool, choosing and reevaluating firms as circumstances warrant. Assignments consider estimated total cost, timeframe, strategy, capabilities and relevant-market experience; an investment manager may be used instead. Each assignment needs written Executive Director or designee approval and a signed Transition Notice. Services may include cross-asset trading, exposure and tracking-error management, appropriate derivatives or ETFs, and full cost and trading reports. Managers provide post-trade cost and efficiency analyses; staff report annual activity to the Investment Committee. Distributed securities and foreign currencies are liquidated or converted orderly to maximize value; staff may choose alternatives to the distributing broker or custodian with required approval.

result.title: XIII. Performance Benchmarks
result.summary: TRS’s total-return objective, based on actuarial advice, is at least 7% annually; performance versus this obligation is most useful over 5–30 years. Long-term policy benchmarks allocate 37% public equity (MSCI ACWI Investable Market), 15% private equity (Russell 3000 + 3%), 15% global income (hedged Bloomberg Barclays Aggregate), 8% private credit (50/50 high-yield and leveraged-loan indices), 16% real estate (TRS index), 2% other real assets (CPI + 5%), 6% diversifying strategies (T-bills + 4%), and 1% short-term investments (91-day T-bills). The interim index keeps the same benchmarks and weights except diversifying strategies at 5% and short-term investments at 2%; it will be adjusted as long-term targets are approached. Benchmarks support market, actuarial-assumption, and peer comparisons and are reviewed annually or through asset-class tactical reviews. Strategic tilts should be assessed over full economic cycles. Individual managers are judged on risk-adjusted and nominal market-relative returns, style-group peers, style adherence, and policy compliance—not the aggregate objective. Staff and consultants implement strategy, oversee managers, monitor/report performance, and update the Board as scheduled, requested, or necessary.

result.title: XIV. Custodial Credit Risk
result.summary: Under Illinois Pension Code §§16-179 and 16-181, the TRS Board of Trustees may act as trustee of Article 16 reserves and deposit trust funds with banks, savings and loan associations, or trust companies. The policy defines credit risk as a counterparty’s failure to meet obligations and custodial credit risk as possible loss of deposits or investments if a financial institution fails. TRS mitigates custodial risk by conducting and documenting due diligence on custodians and advisors; setting investment parameters in the policy and manager agreements; annually reviewing the custodian’s financial condition and taking Board-directed action if concerns arise; holding investments in custodial accounts, a custodian nominee’s name, or approved depository/book-entry systems, while following applicable rules for assets held elsewhere; and requiring segregated accounts that do not commingle TRS securities, plus monthly custodian reports. A nominee is the registered holder acting for the beneficial owner, simplifying securities registration and transfer.

result.title: XV. General Investment Restrictions and/or Guidelines
result.summary: Leverage must match the hired investment strategy, follow manager parameters, and be reviewable by Staff, the Consultant, or Investment Committee. Commingled-fund exposure is assessed case by case; reviewed offering documents become allocation guidelines. All investments must comply with Illinois Pension Code restrictions. Policy exceptions require prior Board review and written authorization; unauthorized exceptions must be promptly reported with remedial action. If securities lending is adopted, loans must be fully collateralized, marked to market daily, and periodically reported; the agent selects and monitors borrowers (with the System able to prohibit borrowers), and lending must not disrupt other managers. Cash-holding managers should remain invested, subject to specified transition, authorization, or cash-mandate exceptions. The Board establishes rebalancing policy and delegates operations to Staff. The Board supports use of qualified, fairly compensating, non-debarred responsible contractors, subject to fiduciary duties. Staff may hedge currency risk or actively manage it for return; benchmarks remain unhedged, and managers need not hedge.

result.title: XVI. Performance Monitoring
result.summary: Performance monitoring relies on periodic reviews from external investment managers, the custodian, consultants, and staff. Managers provide staff-directed reports in the standardized format for public-market separate accounts; other formats may be supplemental, and managers may be asked to present to staff, consultants, or the Board. The custodian reports manager-level and total-fund performance to staff and the consultant, including securities-lending results if applicable. The consultant provides quarterly reports to staff, while the General Consultant reports to the Board at regular meetings, using custodian-reported asset values and performance calculations. Staff ensures reports arrive on time, supervises external reporting, and works with the consultant on a detailed quarterly performance booklet. Its executive summary includes, at minimum, the latest available one-, three-, and five-year periods.

result.title: XVII. Proxy Voting
result.summary: The Board considers active proxy voting an important part of its investment program. Managers must coordinate a proxy-voting program with System Staff, vote in Members’ interests, and maintain records for Staff or service providers upon request or at specified intervals. Staff monitors external Managers’ voting practices, with possible assistance from external service providers, to assess compliance with fiduciary responsibilities. Staff submits an annual report to the Board after the June 30 fiscal year-end, detailing for each applicable Manager ballots cast, issues voted, and percentages voted with or against management or abstained; the TRS website also publishes an annual fiduciary report covering proxy-voting management. When Staff votes proxies, such as during asset transitions, it votes with management unless the Executive Director directs otherwise.

result.title: XVIII. Brokerage Expense Management
result.summary: The policy supersedes prior brokerage policies and delegates securities-trading placement and execution to managers, subject to fiduciary duties and best-execution requirements in their Investment Management Agreements. Equity managers must scrutinize brokerage costs and, upon request, report System transactions; the custodian also provides brokerage information to Staff. Soft dollars are permitted under Section 28(e), but managers must report quarterly to Staff the shares traded, commission amounts, brokerage firms, and goods or services received. The System will not use internal soft-dollar accounts for vendor payments; external managers may use soft dollars with required disclosures, and all such dollars belong to the System. Managers must manage commission expenses effectively. Staff will report chronic or material policy violations to the Board and provide an annual brokerage-activity summary, including directed brokerage.

result.title: XIX. Sustainability Policy Statement
result.summary: TRS considers material, relevant, decision-useful sustainability factors in investment decisions, subject to financial and fiduciary prudence. Factors include corporate governance and leadership, environmental and social capital, human capital, and business model and innovation. TRS periodically evaluates their relevance to its portfolio and changing markets, and monitors investment managers to encourage their integration. Each year, TRS publishes a website fiduciary report under the Illinois Sustainable Investing Act addressing its sustainable investment strategy; assessment of portfolio-wide systemic and regulatory risks and opportunities, including sustainability factors; managers’ integration of these factors; proxy voting; and corporate engagement and other stewardship activities.

result.title: XX. Improving Access to the TRS Investment Process
result.summary: The policy formalizes TRS Board direction to increase use of minority- and women-owned businesses (MWBEs), building on gains since FY2000, through measurable goals and annual effectiveness reviews (more often if warranted). MWBE status follows Illinois law; manager allocations must meet fiduciary standards, and brokerage rates must be market-competitive. For FY2024, public-markets managers’ MWBE brokerage objectives are 35% domestic equities, 17% international equities, and 17% global income. Managers report quarterly on all transactions benefiting MWBE brokers; Investment Staff monitor and report findings, may seek discussions or Watch List placement, and provide written expectations at key engagement stages. The FY2024 MWBE investment-manager target is 22% of total fund assets. Under state law, the Board sets asset and fee diversity goals by asset class, and the best-qualified MWBE firm meeting search criteria must be presented as a finalist in public-manager searches. Staff report progress and actions semiannually. Before transition-management contracts, the CIO reviews proposed MWBE brokerage use. The Investment Committee oversees utilization, and its Chair coordinates with the Consultant on MWBE inclusion in searches.

result.title: XXI. Emerging Managers Program
result.summary: The Emerging Managers Program establishes transparent, documented, objective decisions in beneficiaries’ best interests and builds relationships with promising smaller, developing, minority-owned, female-owned, and Illinois-based managers across public and private markets. Launched with a $500 million commitment in 2005, it now exceeds $1 billion and may lead to full TRS mandates. Staff maintain and assess a manager universe, gather detailed information, conduct due diligence, and recommend candidates to the applicable Oversight Committee; approved recommendations are reported to the Investment Committee. Initial and subsequent funding consider portfolio fit, diversification, risk and return, and organizational capacity. The Program does not alter long-term allocation targets and is exempt from systematic rebalancing. Search documents and agreements specify performance expectations, risks, qualitative assessments, benchmarks or peers, and fees. Staff monitor results, conduct periodic due diligence, and report material events. Managers may graduate or be terminated, with reimbursement to the Program; private-market decisions generally occur within two to five years. Termination grounds, evaluations, documentation, approvals, and asset transitions are specified.

nodes.title: Introduction
nodes.summary: TRS Trustees established Emerging Managers Program guidelines requiring transparent decision-making, objective evaluation, proper documentation, and decisions solely in participants’ and beneficiaries’ best interests. The Program seeks long-term relationships with growing managers that have smaller asset bases and developing track records, firms with strong investment approaches but limited marketing outreach, and minority-owned, female-owned, and Illinois-based managers. In May 2005, the Board committed $500 million—about 1.5% of the Fund at the time, sourced from the domestic large-cap index fund. Total Program commitments now exceed $1 billion. It covers public and private markets, with evaluation criteria tailored to each asset class, and aims to enable superior-performing emerging managers eventually to receive full TRS investment allocations.

nodes.title: Search and Selection Process
nodes.summary: The Program selects emerging investment managers through five steps: (1) Staff maintains and updates an ongoing universe of managers, inviting firms to submit standardized information via TRS’s website or Staff; (2) Staff periodically assesses candidates against TRS criteria and portfolio needs; (3) promising candidates provide further details on their organization, philosophy, process, personnel, risk controls, performance, and fees; (4) Staff meets management and conducts due diligence on staffing, policies, technology, risk management, and compliance, incorporating available Consultant analysis; and (5) Staff recommends candidates to the relevant Oversight Committee for approval, favoring firms with strong quantitative and qualitative prospects over three to five years and potential to become full TRS mandates. Approved recommendations may be implemented, with reports and a policy-compliance checklist provided to the Investment Committee at its next scheduled meeting. A full TRS mandate moves a manager out of the Program into the overall portfolio and is typically larger and important to asset-class and investment-style diversification.

nodes.title: Initial Funding
nodes.summary: Initial funding recommendations go to the applicable Staff Oversight Committee and consider asset class and diversification, strategy and long-term fit with TRS, risk/return profile, and the firm’s scale, depth, and institutionalization plans. The Emerging Manager Program does not change the Fund’s long-term allocation targets and is exempt from systematic rebalancing; it aims to build relationships with managers who may later receive full TRS mandates. Additional funding or withdrawals are based on ongoing Staff and Consultant analysis, with formal recommendations to the Committee as appropriate. For delegated external-provider hiring, the Investment Committee and Board oversee compliance with established Pension Code, administrative-rule, and Investment Policy processes. The Chair and members may request supporting documentation. Staff, the Consultant, and the applicable Committee review whether recommendations were fairly based and screening consistently applied. Candidates may be asked to present formally to the Committee.

nodes.title: Defining Expectations
nodes.summary:
Defining Expectations
In the case where a manager is hired, the search process document shall include, but may not be limited to, the following:
1. a summary of performance criteria considerations, 2. the absolute and relative risks inherent in the manager’s approach, 3. staff’s qualitative assessment, and
4. identification of relevant comparative measures such as benchmarks and/or peer samples, and proposed fee structure.
Staff and Consultant shall incorporate the relevant factors related to expectations of the manager into the executed Investment Management Agreement.

nodes.title: Board Reporting and Monitoring
nodes.summary:
Board Reporting and Monitoring
After a manager is selected to the Program, Staff will regularly monitor the manager’s results versus expectations. Staff will conduct periodic due diligence meetings with the outside organizations and may provide the Board with reports summarizing the assessments made. All material events regarding an investment manager will be communicated to the applicable Staff Oversight Committee and, when deemed necessary, to the Board.
Page 44Investment Policy July 1, 2024

nodes.title: Program Funding: Graduation/Termination
nodes.summary: Staff may recommend graduating a mandate into the TRS investment portfolio based on the manager’s Program performance and development of its organization. The recommendation and due diligence go to the applicable Staff Oversight Committee for approval. Upon graduation, the Program is reimbursed an amount equal to the manager’s initial funding. Termination generally carries the same reimbursement requirement unless otherwise stated. Because private-market investments have longer commitment periods, staff provide a graduation or termination recommendation to the committee within two to five years of the initial investment. If approved, the investment is removed from the Program and reimbursement is completed as described above.

nodes.title: Termination Guidelines
nodes.summary: The guidelines identify grounds for terminating TRS investment managers, including ownership or personnel changes, client or asset losses, shifts in philosophy or process, poor responsiveness or performance, changes in TRS strategy, policy violations, approved new approaches, and diversification needs. The list is not exhaustive; decisions depend on each case’s facts. Because the Program develops emerging managers, allocations may be redirected if a manager is not progressing toward managing a full institutional mandate. Before deciding, relevant considerations must be identified, described, ranked, and evaluated quantitatively and qualitatively. Documentation should explain the reasons and supporting issues, assumptions, results, and, where appropriate, risks, costs, and expected benefits. Staff and the Consultant, with Staff Oversight Committee approval, may initiate termination for public-markets emerging managers meeting Watch List criteria or other immediate concerns. With committee approval, Staff transitions assets to a search finalist, another TRS manager, passive index management, or cash, and reports to the Investment Committee and Board at their next meeting.

result.title: XXII. Recovery of Investment Losses
result.summary: The Board’s policy is to recover investment losses consistent with its fiduciary duties. For potentially recoverable securities class actions, the System participates as a class member; its master trustee or designee files claims and supporting documents to secure its pro rata recovery, consulting litigation counsel if unable to do so. The designee maintains and follows procedures for identifying cases, eligible transactions and accounts, and filing claims. Investment Staff monitors compliance, checks that notices received by the System are captured, and periodically reports recoveries to the Board. The Board may pursue lead-plaintiff status or independent litigation if active involvement adds value without harming the System, after consultation with relevant internal and external advisers. In bankruptcy proceedings involving System assets, the responsible investment manager must notify the System and seek entitled distributions or relief; Staff monitors the manager and master trustee and reports such proceedings quarterly. The policy was adopted in 2000 and amended or revised repeatedly, most recently July 1, 2024.
